{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=preference+formation+path+dependence+longitudinal+behavior+active+learning&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"title\": [\"Public Transit Path Choice Modeling with Behavior Driven Preference Learning: An Interpretable Framework\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Public transit path choice behavior modeling is fundamental to travel demand analysis and transit guidance strategies. Discrete choice models based on Multinomial Logit remain the dominant approach for path choice analysis, yet predictive accuracy is frequently constrained by underlying assumptions; conversely, the few exiting deep learning-based methods suffer from weak interpretability. More importantly, neither method effectively captures individual preferences, making it difficult to reflect traveler heterogeneity. To address these limitations, a behavior-driven preference learning-based public transit path choice model is proposed in this study. First, individual behavioral features are constructed using historical data, and a preference mining layer is designed to learn latent preference representations from long-term historical behaviors. Then, gating mechanisms and attention mechanisms are introduced to achieve differentiated attention to path features among different travelers. Furthermore, a comprehensive model interpretation framework is developed by leveraging methods such as Accumulated Local Effects, Integrated Gradients, and Adaptive Clustering. Finally, empirical studies are conducted based on real-world data from Beijing, and comparative analyses with existing methods are performed. Performance analysis results indicate that an accuracy rate of 83.90% is achieved by the proposed model, representing a improvement of 11.86 percentage points. Furthermore, it is demonstrated through interpretability analyses that complex nonlinear relationships among intricate path features, contextual features, and individual preferences can be more effectively captured. Additionally, the distinctly different decision-making logics exhibited by various preference groups during the path choice process are reasonably explained.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1006/game.1996.0032\", \"title\": [\"Path Dependence and Learning from Neighbors\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0032\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1996, 4]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.2380309\", \"title\": [\"Habit Formation and Risk Preference Dependence\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2380309\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2014]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7540068\", \"title\": [\"Attractor-Weighted Neuromodulation of Reward Path Dependence and Habit Formation\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper proposes a formal dynamical-systems theory of reward-seeking path dependence in the brain. The central claim is that repeated reward-seeking does not merely increase or decrease dopamine in a colloquial sense; rather, it reshapes a multiscale state space in which action sequences become attractors, habit chunks, and context-sensitive policy priors. The model is built on three established empirical commitments: first, midbrain dopamine neurons encode reward prediction error rather than pleasure itself; second, dopamine contributes more to wanting than liking ; and third, cortico-striatal circuits progressively chunk repeated actions into stable habit-like sequences. We extend these findings into a multineuromodulator model in which dopamine, opioids, serotonin, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine jointly regulate incentive salience, hedonic impact, temporal discounting, and uncertainty. The resulting theory explains why some reward paths intensify into compulsive attractors, why devaluation does not automatically terminate them, and why transitions to alternative behavioral regimes depend on a stability shift in the underlying attractor landscape rather than on a simple drop in reward.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7540068\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "1d592f6f7034564bd1518eb2c734ce82e80bc6888fe260e9efc0d2302e53023a", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7331065", "doi:10.1006/game.1996.0032", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.2380309", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7540068"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7331065", "https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0032", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2380309", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7540068"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
